prompt.context: After returning from a trade show, the CEO of a large grocery distribution center calls you. He enthusiastically describes a new technology which could be used to automate part of his company's process. Knowing that this CEO is a tech-enthusiast who loves innovation for the novelty of it, you ponder the implications.
prompt.question: How would you tackle this problem? Should the company automate part of its distribution process?

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have a specific goal or target return in mind?
clarifying_info.a: No specific goal. The CEO trusts us and will do whatever we advise. This is to test business judgment.

clarifying_info.q: How many shipments does the company make and to how many stores?
clarifying_info.a: Shipments are made to roughly 50 grocery stores in the immediate area, and the company does 1 million shipments per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to automate?
clarifying_info.a: There is a one-time outlay of $4M, plus recurring overhead, training, and additional maintenance costs of $1.0M per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the three phases of the distribution process?
clarifying_info.a: The three phases are: 1) Receiving, 2) Holding & Picking, 3) Shipping.

clarifying_info.q: How many hours per week does each employee work?
clarifying_info.a: Each employee works 40 hours per week.

clarifying_info.q: What is employee pay per hour in each function?

exhibits.title: Current Distribution Process — Hours by Phase
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the three distribution phases (Receiving, Holding & Packing, Shipping) with the total hours per week currently required in each phase.

data.note: All units are hours per week

exhibits.title: Automated Distribution Process — Hours by Phase
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the same three distribution phases showing the hours per week required after automation is implemented.

framework: Revenues: Recognize this is primarily a cost issue — the company is not experiencing capacity issues and satisfying current customer demand, so automating will not generate additional revenues
Costs — Existing: Fixed costs (rent/mortgage/leases, overhead, salaries) and Variable costs (hourly employees, repairs & maintenance, inventory holding, shipping)
Costs — Incremental One-Time: Initial cost of automating ($4M), cost of initial training, severance pay for terminated employees
Costs — Incremental Ongoing: Annual servicing/repairs and additional facility costs (energy, insurance, etc.) — $1.0M/year
Product: Consider changes to product quality (none) and ability to distribute additional product types (none)
Other: Potential future synergies (e.g., new technology interfacing with future tech) and impact on relationships with employees, grocers, and/or suppliers

questions.prompt: Visualize and describe the distribution process flow for a grocery distribution center. What are the key phases and cost drivers in each?
questions.guidance: Candidate should walk through the process from receiving goods, holding and picking orders, to shipping. They should identify labor, equipment (forklifts), insurance, and storage (cold and dry) as key cost drivers in each phase. If the candidate does not volunteer this, press them to do so before revealing the exhibit.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total number of employees required in each function and the total annual labor cost under the current (pre-automation) process.
questions.guidance: Candidate divides total weekly hours by 40 hours/employee to get headcount, multiplies by hourly rate for weekly cost, sums all functions, then multiplies by 52 weeks. They should use 52 weeks (not 50).

math.setup: Employees = Total Hours / 40 hrs per employee; Weekly Cost = Employees x Hourly Rate; Annual Cost = Total Weekly Cost x 52
math.answer: Current annual labor cost: $12,272,000; Total employees: 375

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the new number of employees required and total annual labor cost after automation. What is the annual labor savings?
questions.guidance: Candidate applies the same method to the new hours in Exhibit 2, then subtracts new annual cost from current annual cost to derive annual savings. Key insight: Shipping hours increase (automation may shift work), while Holding & Picking drops significantly. Receiving is unchanged.

math.setup: Same method as above applied to Exhibit 2 hours, then Annual Savings = Current Cost - New Cost
steps: Employee decrease: 375 - 331.25 = ~44 employees (Holding & Picking loses ~119, Shipping gains ~75)
math.answer: New annual labor cost: $10,257,000; Annual labor savings: $2,015,000; Net reduction of ~44 employees

questions.prompt: Calculate the break-even period for the automation investment.
questions.guidance: Candidate should net the annual labor savings against the recurring incremental costs to get annual incremental contribution margin, then divide the one-time outlay by this figure. The break-even is ~3.9 years. Strong candidates then evaluate whether this payback period is attractive given the context — especially that the CEO may be motivated by novelty rather than financial discipline.

math.setup: Annual Incremental CM = Annual Labor Savings - Annual Incremental Costs; Break-Even Years = One-Time Outlay / Annual Incremental CM

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential costs associated with each phase of the distribution process (Receiving, Holding & Picking, Shipping)?

ideas: Space for automated systems vs. manual workstations

ideas: Ongoing training for staff on new systems

categories.name: Other Operational
ideas: Impact on shipment accuracy and error rates

recommendation: The break-even on automation is approximately 3.9 years, driven by ~$2.0M in annual labor savings versus $1.0M in annual incremental costs against a $4.0M one-time investment

Given the CEO's motivation appears to be enthusiasm for innovation rather than financial necessity, the firm should proceed cautiously — the investment is financially sound if the company has the cash and a 4-year horizon, but management should be clear this is a financial decision, not a novelty purchase
risks: The CEO's tech-enthusiasm may cloud objective financial judgment; automation for novelty rather than need increases execution risk
Shipping labor hours increase post-automation (from 75 to 150 employees), suggesting automation shifts — not eliminates — some labor burden
44 employees displaced creates HR and morale risk; severance costs not yet factored into the break-even
Technology risk: new automation systems may have unexpected downtime or integration issues during ramp-up
next_steps: Validate the projected post-automation hours in Exhibit 2 with the technology vendor
Model severance costs for ~119 displaced Holding & Picking workers and add to one-time outlay
Assess the company's liquidity to fund the $4M outlay without constraining operations
Evaluate whether the technology is future-compatible (interfaces with other potential systems) to justify the investment beyond current labor savings
